transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-08
Start: 11:00 AM ET
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Aaron Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Aurora Bank - Head of AI), Priya Desai (Platform Eng), Marcus Hale (SRE), Nadia (PM)

Summary:
Quick sync on this week's latency tuning experiments: TTFT improvements from streaming changes, sequence length profiling, and kernel selection tradeoffs. Agreed next steps around data share and a potential on-site benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, umm we were hoping to run through the results from this week's runs, focu — focus on TTFT and tail latencies. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Liam: Good, thanks. Yeah we've got Priya and Marcus on the line, so we'll hand it over for the deep stuff.
[00:15] Priya: Morning. We've been seeing the same pattern, TTFT spikes on cold requests, and tails when sequence length jumps above 768 tokens.
[00:25] Aaron: Right, so this week we tested two changes: enabling streaming early flush and switching kernel set from default cuDNN to our Triton custom fused-attn kernels for the pico config. The streaming change affects first-byte latency primarily.
[00:40] Marcus: Quick question, Aaron — were you running with kv-cache warm enabled for the majority of these runs? I know that makes a big difference.
[00:47] Aaron: Yes, all runs had KV cache warmed for 60% of requests. We kept a controlled mix: 60% warm, 40% cold to mimic your reported traffic.
[00:55] [01:05] Sofia: Cool, can you share the headline numbers first? TTFT, p95, p99 for the 512 token baseline and then after changes?
[01:12] Aaron: Sure. Baseline (float16, cuDNN kernels, non-streaming): TTFT median ~1.35s, p95 ~2.9s, p99 ~4.6s for 512 tokens. After enabling streaming only: median TTFT dropped to ~0.82s, p95 ~1.6s, p99 ~2.9s. After switching to Triton fused kernels (plus streaming): median ~0.70s, p95 ~1.3s, p99 ~2.2s. Cost delta: Triton kernels add ~6% infra cost due to slightly higher GPU occupancy in these configs but reduce overall token time so net unit cost roughly flat.
[02:00] Liam: That's promising. The p99 drop is what we care about. Did you see any accuracy regressions or output truncation when streaming was on?
[02:12] Aaron: We instrumented the output and ran n-gram overlap checks; negligible differences for your prompt set. There's a tiny risk in some tool-calling flows since streaming flushes partial tokens, but we can use structured streaming boundaries to avoid.
[02:28] Priya: When you say streaming early flush, is that the server-side chunking at token 1 or token 4? We currently have a client-side stream consumer that expects a first chunk immediately.
[02:40] Aaron: We used a chunk size of 1 token for TTFT numbers; but for production we often recommend chunking of 4 tokens to reduce RPC overhead. The 1-token gives best TTFT but increases network chatter.
[02:52] Nadia: Quick clarification — our average sequence length is actually around 220 tokens for chat prompts but with a 5% tail over 800 tokens from long transcripts. We'll upload the histogram.
[03:05] Sofia: That's helpful; the sequence length distribution matters a lot for kernel selection because fused kernels shine at mid-range lengths but cold-start and very long sequences stress memory and kernel fallback paths.
[03:20] Aaron: Exactly. We also did an experiment with quantization: int8 (AWQ-like) reduced p99 by another ~10% on the large GPU but increased variance a bit and required calibration. So it's a tradeoff.
[03:38] Marcus: Any complications on the KV cache with int8? We've had bugs before where cached key/value shapes were subtly different in quantized kernels.
[03:45] Aaron: We observed no shape diffs — all cache hits align — but we did have to add a small dequantize path for some attention matmul ops. That's part of our recommended patch for int8. We'll include the patch notes.
[03:58] [04:05] Liam: About kernel selection: what determines when you pick Triton fused vs cuDNN? Is it automatic?
[04:13] Aaron: Our runtime uses a kernel selector that considers model size, sequence length distribution, and latency SLO. For this POC we forced Triton for the mid-length bucket (128-1024). The selector can be policy driven — e.g., prefer low-cost kernels for non-SLA traffic.
[04:31] Priya: If the selector is dynamic, do we get consistent behavior across Dedicated and Private deployments? We're concerned about test reproducibility across environments.
[04:40] Sofia: Good point. For Dedicated and Private we can pin a kernel policy in the deployment config so the selector becomes deterministic for a rollout. We recommended pinning during the POC to avoid drift.
[04:55] Marcus: On the subject of determinism, did you see any variability across GPU types? We have a mix of A100 and H100 in our lab.
[05:03] Aaron: Yes. H100 gave slightly better p50 with int8 and fused kernels, H100's SM architecture favors the fused attention. A100 still decent but Triton kernels require tuning flags for best perf. We'll add a per-GPU note in the doc.
[05:18] Liam: Ok, what about throughput and batching? We're sensitive to cost so we want aggressvie batching but not at the expense of TTFT.
[05:26] Aaron: We measured batching tradeoffs: target batch size of 8 gave best throughput but increased median TTFT by ~200ms. We implemented adaptive batching where we allow small batches up to 4 for SLA traffic and higher batch sizes for background workloads. That preserves TTFT while improving throughput for non-SLA routes.
[05:44] Priya: Would adaptive batching be handled by Redwood runtime automatically or do we need to set per-route configs?
[05:50] Aaron: Runtime handles it; you can also override per-route. We'll show the config snippet.
[05:55] [06:05] Nadia: Security question — if we want to test on your Private stack with our KMS (customer-managed), will that affect perf? We've seen extra hops add latency.
[06:15] Sofia: Good callout. We support customer-managed KMS using a local HSM or cloud KMS; the critical path is token fetch for model keys which we cache. In practice KMS overhead is sub-50ms per key fetch and most requests hit the cache, so negligible on TTFT if configured correctly. But we'll confirm with Marcus's environment.
[06:34] Marcus: I'll set aside a window to test SSO/KMS next week.
[06:38] Aaron: Another note — we saw some memcopy overhead in the cuDNN path that contributed ~70-120ms to p95; Triton fused kernels reduce that by avoiding some host-device round trips. That's part of why p95 improved.
[06:54] Liam: Any known issues with streaming and tool-calls in our payment flow? We have a tool that expects complete JSON output.
[07:02] Aaron: For structured tool output we recommend delimiting with function-call style outputs and using streaming with chunking of 4 tokens and end-of-function markers. We'll include a sample. Streaming can be disabled per-route if you prefer full responses.
[07:18] Priya: Can you also remind us about warm-up requirements for KV cache? We prefer not to run a large warm-up every day.
[07:26] Aaron: We typically use a lightweight prefix cache and keep a rolling warm set. For your traffic 30-60 minutes of background warm traffic is enough to keep hot keys warm. We'll provide a warmup script you can run in your staging cluster.
[07:40] [07:50] Sofia: Quick recap — the combination of streaming + Triton kernels is our recommended path for TTFT and p99 reduction. Next steps: share the perf sheet, you share sequence histograms, plan for an on-site benchmark if numbers still differ. Any objections?
[08:05] Liam: No objections. Sounds like a plan. One ask — include 95/99 tail latencies per-GPU in the sheet.
[08:12] Aaron: Will do.
[08:15] Nadia: And include a note about fallback policies — we want graceful degradation to smaller models when capacity is tight.
[08:22] Sofia: Yes, we'll include routing policy examples (canary, fallback to cheaper model variant).
[08:28] Priya: Also please include a sample config for pinning kernel selection in Private deployments.
[08:33] Aaron: I'll prepare that and the kernel tuning flags.
[08:36] [08:45] Action items (verbatim): Sofia to send perf spreadsheet and pricing options by Friday (2026-12-10). Aaron to send kernel notes and Triton logs by Thursday (2026-12-09). Priya to send sequence length distribution by Saturday (2026-12-11). Marcus to confirm SSO/KMS test window by Sunday (2026-12-12).
[08:58] Sofia: Great, thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and Slack with the artifacts.
[09:03] Liam: Thanks all.
[09:06] Meeting end.
